setupSteps: Warm up first. 2 to 3 minutes of gentle movement (a few cat-cows, ankle circles, easy knee hugs), or do the pose after other poses. Never stretch cold.
Floor. Flat mat or carpeted floor; avoid slippery tiles with bare skin.

Sit on a prop. Place a folded blanket or firm cushion about 5 to 10 cm thick (est.) under the sitting bones. Sources explain that raising the hips above the knees makes it easier to tip the pelvis forward, which is what the pose needs.

Legs. Stretch both legs straight in front, feet together or a few cm apart, toes pointing up. If the hamstrings or lower back pull, bend the knees softly or place a rolled blanket under the knees (sources suggest both).
Sit tall. Press the sitting bones down, lengthen the spine up (Dandasana, Staff pose), hands beside the hips.
Strap or towel (optional). Loop it around the balls of both feet and hold the ends like reins, elbows slightly bent. Use it whenever the hands cannot reach the feet without rounding the back.
Clothing. Stretchy pants; no tight jeans; a fitted top so the camera sees the shoulder and hip.
Camera. Phone on the floor or a low stool at about hip height (about 40 to 60 cm, est.), about 2 m to the side, so the whole body from head to feet is in frame (see sections 11 and 12).

steps.title: Sit tall
steps.action: sit on the blanket with legs forward, spine long, hands by the hips.
steps.feel: sitting bones pressing down, crown of the head lifting.

steps.title: Flex the feet
steps.action: draw the toes toward the shins and press lightly through the heels.
steps.feel: a light stretch in the calves; the thighs gently awake.

steps.title: Soften the knees if needed
steps.action: let the knees bend a small amount, or place the roll under them; keep them softly bent for the whole pose if the back of the legs pull.
steps.feel: pull in the hamstrings easing; the pelvis free to tip forward.

steps.title: Lengthen on an in-breath
steps.action: breathe in and lift the chest, reaching the arms forward (or up beside the ears).
steps.feel: the spine growing taller, the ribs lifting away from the belly.

steps.title: Hinge from the hips
steps.action: breathe out and tip the pelvis forward, leading with the chest, as if folding at the hip joint, not at the waist.
steps.feel: a pull in the hamstrings and, lightly, along the back; the belly moving toward the thighs.

steps.title: Reach only as far as the back stays long
steps.action: rest the hands on the shins, ankles, feet or on the strap, wherever the spine can stay long.
steps.feel: a comfortable stretch, about 4 to 5 out of 10, no pain.

steps.title: Hold
steps.action: stay with slow nose breaths. Beginners about 5 breaths (about 30 seconds, est.); sources range from a few breaths to 30 seconds, with The Yoga Institute suggesting building up toward 1 to 2 minutes.
steps.feel: slow release of the hamstrings; with each out-breath a tiny bit more fold, never forced.
steps.breathing: slow nose breaths; count each out-breath; never hold the breath.

steps.title: Ease out slowly
steps.action: on an in-breath, lengthen the chest forward and up, then roll up with a long spine; the hands slide back to the floor beside the hips.
steps.feel: the back muscles lifting you; no dizziness.

steps.title: Rest
steps.action: sit tall or lean back on the hands; shake out the legs or hug the knees.

commonMistakes.title: Rounding the back to reach the toes
commonMistakes.text: Rounding the back to reach the toes. It loads the lower back and discs, and takes the stretch off the hamstrings. Fix: hinge from the hips, use a strap, bend the knees, reach only as far as the back stays long.

commonMistakes.title: Sitting flat on the floor with a tucked pelvis
commonMistakes.text: Sitting flat on the floor with a tucked pelvis. The pelvis cannot tip forward, so the back rounds. Fix: sit on a folded blanket so the hips are higher than the knees.

commonMistakes.title: Locking or hyperextending the knees
commonMistakes.text: Locking or hyperextending the knees. It can strain the back of the knee. Fix: keep a soft bend in the knees.

commonMistakes.title: Yanking with the strap or arms
commonMistakes.text: Yanking with the strap or arms. Pulling hard forces the stretch and risks a hamstring strain. Fix: hold lightly and let the out-breath do the work.

commonMistakes.title: Bouncing or forcing deeper
commonMistakes.text: Bouncing or forcing deeper. Fast pulses can overstretch the muscle. Fix: stay still, add depth only with each exhale, no pain.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. It raises effort and tension. Fix: slow nose breaths; count out-breaths.

commonMistakes.title: Chasing the forehead to the knees (or toes touching) as the goal
commonMistakes.text: Chasing the forehead to the knees (or toes touching) as the goal. It leads to rounding. Fix: aim for a long spine, not a touch.

commonMistakes.title: Coming up fast
commonMistakes.text: Coming up fast. Dizziness can follow, especially with low or high blood pressure. Fix: lengthen the chest forward first, then rise slowly on an in-breath.

commonMistakes.title: Stretching cold or one-sided
commonMistakes.text: Stretching cold or one-sided. Stiff muscles resist; uneven pulling twists the pelvis. Fix: warm up; keep both sitting bones heavy and level.

safetyNotes: Mild stretch, never pain. A pull at the back of the thighs is normal; sharp pain, a pinch in the back or knee, or tingling is not.

Back and discs: forward flexion of the spine loads the lower back; the NIOS manual says people with sciatica, slip disc or any back problems should avoid this asana, and teaching sources list disc problems, sacroiliac pain and sciatica as contraindications (snippets). Healthline notes a seated forward bend with a rounded spine can strain the low back and irritate the sciatic nerve (snippet). If the doctor allows it, hinge from the hips with a neutral spine, bend the knees and use a strap.

Osteoporosis: a 2013 review (International Journal of Yoga Therapy; seen as a snippet) concluded that movements with spinal flexion can raise the risk of vertebral compression fractures; some sources attribute similar advice to the National Osteoporosis Foundation (secondary reports only). Ask a doctor; if cleared, keep the spine long and fold from the hips only.

Pregnancy: teaching sources list the second and third trimesters as a precaution for this pose (snippets). If cleared by a doctor or midwife, sit with the legs wide apart, do not compress the belly and do not lie flat on the back for long after about 20 weeks (ACOG concern as quoted by Lamaze; snippet).

Blood pressure: sources disagree on gentle forward folds for high blood pressure; Harvard Health stresses care with poses where the head is below the heart and advises checking with a doctor (snippet); this seated fold keeps the head near hip level. Move slowly, do not hold the breath, come up slowly.
Hamstring injury: avoid stretching a recent hamstring strain; stop at sharp pain.
Stop immediately if you feel: sharp back or leg pain, numbness or tingling down the leg, dizziness, a pop or pull in the back of the thigh, chest pain or breathlessness.
Spotter: not needed. Gym etiquette: keep the mat and strap out of the walkway; do not hog a stretching area.

Hold time: about 30 seconds building to 1 to 2 minutes (Yoga Institute) versus 3 to 5 rounds (NIOS). We chose 5 breaths (about 30 s, est.).
Straight versus bent knees: classical straight legs versus modern soft knees or a roll. We chose soft knees for beginners.
Touching toes versus a long spine: traditional goal versus a hinge with a strap. We chose the long spine.
Back conditions: NIOS says avoid with sciatica, slip disc or back problems; modern sources allow a modified hinge. We chose "ask a doctor; do not round; stop at leg symptoms".

Not found: MDNIY technique page; confirmation that the pose is in the AYUSH CYP (it did not appear in retrieved text); a pose-specific MET; measured joint-angle norms; the full text of the osteoporosis and hamstring trials; ACOG pose-specific wording; clinical sources for cholesterol, thyroid, heart disease, postpartum, surgery for this pose; Harvard Health text on forward folds (paywalled). Our thresholds are estimates.
Most pages were seen only as search snippets or summaries; direct page fetches were not possible.
